en: You recently joined Anthropic, and you have a pretty amazing career. I know you started as an entrepreneur, then you took the blue pill and went to Amazon, and then you kind of took the red pill and went back to building. Amandeep Khurana, Member of Technical Staff at Anthropic.

en: To be free of a game, you have to first win the game, and only then do you realize the futility of the game, and then you're free of it. The thing that's missing there is... Introduction

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Amandeep Khurana, who leads a team inside Anthropic's forward deployed engineering function. He's also a friend, so this is a first: we've had 100 private conversations and zero public ones. His path is unusual: engineer at AWS, solutions architect at Cloudera, founded a company that exited to Databricks, then five and a half years at Amazon, where he voluntarily gave up his management role in 2023 to go back to being an IC. The things we'll cover: what a forward deployed engineer actually is versus renamed professional services, the three filters they use to decide which customers to take, turning down offers worth two to three times more and why, on winning the game before you can quit it and where that advice breaks, and why everyone at Anthropic has the same title, including Karpathy. Let's get into it.
zh: 嘿，我是 Carlos，Product School 的 CEO，也是 The Product Podcast 的主持人。我今天的嘉宾是 Amandeep Khurana，他在 Anthropic 的前置部署工程职能部门领导一个团队。他也是我的朋友，所以这是头一遭：我们有过 100 次私人对话，却零次公开对话。他的路径很不寻常：AWS 工程师，Cloudera 解决方案架构师，创办了一家被 Databricks 收购的公司，然后在亚马逊待了五年半，2023 年他主动放弃了管理职位，回归成为 IC。我们将涵盖的内容：前置部署工程师到底是什么， versus 改名的专业服务；他们用来决定接哪些客户的三个过滤器；拒绝价值两到三倍的 offer 以及为什么；关于先赢得游戏才能退出游戏，以及这个建议在哪里失效；还有为什么 Anthropic 人人头衔相同，包括 Karpathy。开始吧。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Welcome to The Product Podcast, Amandeep.
zh: 欢迎来到 The Product Podcast，Amandeep。

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: Thank you, thank you. I'm excited to be here and excited to spend some time with you.
zh: 谢谢，谢谢。我很兴奋能来到这里，也很兴奋能和你共度一些时间。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: This is a special and weird one for me, because you're my friend, and we've had a ton of conversations about life, AI, and everything in between. But we've never had a public conversation, right? So I just want to acknowledge that.
zh: 这对我来说是一次特别又奇怪的经历，因为你是我的朋友，我们聊过很多关于生活、AI 以及介于两者之间的一切。但我们从未有过一次公开对话，对吧？所以我想先确认这一点。

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: Yeah, thank you, and thank you for the opportunity. It's going to be an interesting one. It'll be fun, and it is a different conversation for sure. From Entrepreneur to Amazon to Anthropic
zh: 是的，谢谢你，也谢谢你给我这个机会。这会是一场有意思的对话。会很好玩的，而且肯定是一次不一样的对话。 从创业者到亚马逊再到 Anthropic

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: You've been a collaborator behind the scenes, and I appreciate that, but I wanted to bring you on stage, especially because you recently joined Anthropic, and you have a pretty amazing career. I know you started as an entrepreneur, then you took the blue pill and went to Amazon, and then you took the red pill and went back to building, but now with Anthropic. So I want to understand a little bit more about that part of your journey.
zh: 你一直是在幕后协助我的人，我很感激，但我想把你请到台前来，尤其是因为你最近加入了 Anthropic，而且你的职业生涯相当了不起。我知道你最初是创业者，然后你吞下了蓝色药丸去了亚马逊，接着你吞下了红色药丸回归打造事业，不过这次是在 Anthropic。所以我想更深入了解一下你旅程中的那一段。

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: Yeah, for sure. Let me give some background context. I trained as an engineer and took up a typical engineering job back in the 2010, 2011 time frame. I went to work for AWS at that time. What I found was that while I enjoyed the engineering work, the hands-on engineering, it just wasn't enough for me. It wasn't really what I truly wanted to do. I got an opportunity to work at a startup and go work with customers, and I had no idea what that entailed. So I took it on and moved to the Valley. The company was called Cloudera. I became a solution architect and did all kinds of customer-facing and partner-facing work there. I spent five years, did a bunch of different projects, worked with a bunch of different customers, and I really loved it. Through that experience, I also learned, just by osmosis, what company building looks like. I had this dream in the back of my mind that I wanted to be a business person at some point, and I don't know where it came from. I think it came from watching my dad build his business. So I wanted to do that. I said, "You know what, I'm in the Valley, the game to be played here is to go build a business." So I started thinking about it, found a set of problems I got excited about, and said, "I'm going to go do this." That's how I started my company, in 2016. That company eventually exited to Databricks. Awesome experience, lots of learnings, lots of ups and downs along the way. In 2020, Covid hit, and I wanted to start another company, but it just didn't happen. I said I need to do something. A friend of mine was at Amazon at the time. He calls me and says, "Hey, you're up to no good, why don't you come here and help me build this line of business?" So I said, fine, whatever ideas I'm working on aren't quite working out, so maybe I'll go do this and not burn through my savings. I joined Amazon and ended up spending five and a half years there, building different kinds of things from the ground up. I did four zero-to-one initiatives, two of them in the AI space. And even there the journey is interesting, because I went from being an IC, to a management role owning both product and engineering, to then giving up all the management responsibilities and becoming an IC product manager back in 2023, because I just wanted to.
zh: 是的，当然。让我先讲一些背景。我受训成为工程师，在 2010、2011 年前后找了一份典型的工程师工作。当时我去了 AWS 工作。我发现，虽然我享受工程工作，享受动手的工程，但它对我来说就是不够。它并不是我真正想做的事情。我得到了一个机会去一家初创公司工作、去和客户打交道，而我完全不知道那意味着什么。于是我接了下来，搬到了硅谷。那家公司叫 Cloudera。我成为了一名解决方案架构师，在那里做了各种面向客户和面向合作伙伴的工作。我待了五年，做了很多不同的项目，和很多不同的客户合作，我非常热爱那段经历。通过那段经历，我还耳濡目染地了解到了打造公司是什么样子。我心里一直藏着一个梦想，就是我某一天想成为一个商业人士，而我不知道它从何而来。我想它来自看着我父亲打造他自己的生意。所以我想去做这件事。我说："你猜怎么着，我在硅谷，这里要玩的游戏就是去打造一门生意。" 于是我开始思考这件事，找到了一批让我兴奋的问题，然后说："我要去做这件事。" 就这样，我在 2016 年创办了我的公司。那家公司最终被 Databricks 收购。很棒的经历，学到了很多，一路上也经历了很多起起落落。2020 年，新冠疫情来了，我想再创办一家公司，但就是没成。我说我得做点什么。我有个朋友当时在亚马逊。他打电话给我说："嘿，你整天游手好闲不干正事，为什么不来这儿帮我打造这条业务线呢？" 于是我说，行吧，反正我在琢磨的那些点子也不太顺利，也许我就去做这个，顺便别把我的积蓄烧光。我加入了亚马逊，最终在那里待了五年半，从零开始打造各种不同的东西。我做了四个从零到一的项目，其中两个在 AI 领域。而且即便在那里，这段旅程也很有意思，因为我从 IC，到担任一个同时负责产品和工程的管理职位，再到 2023 年放弃所有管理职责、成为一名 IC 产品经理，因为我就是想这么做。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I want to stop you there, because it's pretty unique. A lot of times people want to grow in their careers and assume that means managing more people, and you kind of did that as a general manager at Amazon. And then it seems like you chose to go back, quote-unquote, to being an IC. Now it's cool again, right? But I think it wasn't that obvious or cool in 2023, and I want to understand more about that rationale.
zh: 我想在这里打断你一下，因为这非常独特。很多时候人们想要在职业生涯中成长，并认为那意味着管理更多的人，而你在亚马逊作为总经理确实做到了这一点。然后看起来你选择了回归，加引号地说，成为一名 IC。现在这又变酷了，对吧？但我认为在 2023 年那并不那么显而易见或酷，我想更深入了解你当时的那样做的理由。

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: You're right, it wasn't cool. It wasn't something a lot of people were doing. I found myself in a place where there was this opportunity in front of me, which was an IC opportunity, and it was in a domain I wanted to learn and didn't know anything about. If there had been a management opportunity, I might have picked that over the IC opportunity. But I said, "Look, I want to learn this thing. I want to get involved. Let me just jump in and see what happens, and let me learn," because I'm not going to learn a ton if I continue spending a large chunk of my time on org building or management work. I wanted to be hands-on. That was one. Second, I spoke with a few folks at AWS at the time who had done similar transitions, who had gone from a VP role to an IC role and then eventually back into a leadership role. I asked them how they thought about it, and they advised me with some perspectives. So I took that on and said, "I'll give it a shot. I have nothing to lose here. Worst case, I'm going to learn about this new domain. Best case, I'm going to learn about this new domain. And as this team grows, there might be management opportunities I can take on." So that's how I thought about it. It wasn't where it is today. For me, it was: I want to learn that thing, I want to be hands-on, and we'll see what happens.
zh: 你说得对，那时候并不酷。这不是很多人在做的事情。当时我发现自己身处这样一个境地：我面前有一个机会，一个 IC 的机会，而且是在一个我想学习但一无所知的领域。如果当时有一个管理的机会，我可能会选它而不是那个 IC 的机会。但我说："听着，我想学这个东西。我想参与进去。让我跳进去看看会发生什么，让我去学。" 因为如果我继续把大部分时间花在组织建设或管理工作上，我学不到太多东西。我想亲自动手。这是第一点。第二，我当时和 AWS 的几位做过类似转变的人聊过，他们从 VP 职位转到 IC 职位，后来又回到了领导职位。我问他们是怎么想的，他们给了我一些视角和建议。于是我接受了这些建议，说："我会试一试。我在这儿没什么可输的。最坏的情况，我会学到这个新领域。最好的情况，我也会学到这个新领域。而且随着这个团队成长，可能会有我可以承担的管理机会。" 我就是这么想的。它和今天的情况不一样。对我来说，当时就是：我想学那个东西，我想亲自动手，然后我们再看会发生什么。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: So you try it, and I think you liked it, because when you left Amazon, you wanted to either build your own business again or continue working as an IC. But then you didn't choose either of those two.
zh: 所以你试了一下，而且我想你喜欢上了它，因为当你离开亚马逊时，你想的是要么再次打造自己的生意，要么继续做 IC。但后来你两个都没选。

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: That's true. So the story there: I do this thing at Amazon, five and a half years in, and I said, "Okay, I'm ready for something new, and I'm going to go build a company." I made up my mind, I resigned from Amazon. And then about a couple of weeks into it, I get an offer from Anthropic to come in and be part of forward deployed engineering. When that conversation was happening, I did say, "Hey, can you just make me an IC forward deployed engineer? Because this is just so much fun, I want to do this." And the hiring manager for that particular role refused. He said, "No, I want you to come in and lead the team, be a leader on the team." So I said, "Okay, fine, whatever the company needs, we'll make it happen." What Forward Deployed Engineering Actually Is
zh: 是的。那段经历是这样的：我在亚马逊做了这件事，五年半之后，我说："好了，我准备好做点新的事情了，我要去创办一家公司。" 我下定了决心，从亚马逊辞职了。然后大约过了几周，我收到了 Anthropic 的 offer，邀请我加入前置部署工程。在那次对话进行时，我确实说了："嘿，你们能不能就让我做一个 IC 前置部署工程师？因为这实在太好玩了，我就想做这个。" 而那个职位的招聘经理拒绝了。他说："不，我要你进来领导团队，成为团队的一位领导者。" 于是我说："好吧，行，公司需要什么，我们就把它实现。" 前置部署工程到底是什么

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: So tell me more about your current team. What do you really do at Anthropic?
zh: 那么跟我说说你现在的团队。你在 Anthropic 到底做什么？

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: Anthropic had recently started a forward deployed engineering function. Now, we had PhDs, we had people working with customers on implementations, so the concept is not new at Anthropic, but we formalized it as a function relatively recently. I'm part of that function, and I manage a part of it. I've got a bunch of forward deployed engineers working with a number of external and internal initiatives: working with customers, working on internal projects, and really bringing AI into the world in a safe manner, aligned with the charter and mission of the company. These can be projects of all kinds. Internal projects might be, "Oh, there's a new product we're building, let's go try it out," or, "There's a new initiative that impacts Anthropic's operations, so let's bring AI into that." And then, working with customers on identifying use cases that can transform the way they do certain workflows and processes, and then going and building those out. So it's the applied side of AI. Some of the folks also get involved a little bit in the research on the model side of things, but not in the training. It's still once the model is at different stages of its training that people get involved.
zh: Anthropic 最近刚启动了一个前置部署工程职能。其实我们本来就有博士，本来就有和客户一起做落地实施的人，所以这个概念在 Anthropic 并不新鲜，但我们是在相对近期才把它正式化为一个职能。我是这个职能的一部分，管理其中一部分。我手下有一批前置部署工程师，参与许多外部和内部的倡议：和客户合作、做内部项目，真正以安全的方式把 AI 带到世界上，并符合公司的章程和使命。这些项目可以是各种各样的。内部项目可能是："哦，我们正在打造一个新产品，让我们去试一试，" 或者 "有一个影响 Anthropic 运营的新倡议，让我们把 AI 引入其中。" 然后，和客户一起找出能够改变他们某些工作流和流程运转方式的使用场景，然后去把它们构建出来。这就是 AI 的应用侧。有些人也会稍微参与到模型侧的研究中，但不涉及训练。仍然是当模型处于训练的不同阶段时，人们才会参与进来。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: The term forward deployed engineer is super hot now, and a lot of companies doing some sort of enterprise motion claim to have PhDs who go and help the client adopt whatever SaaS tool they're selling. But you guys are the pioneers of this concept, right? So I really want to understand what it really means to do forward deployed engineering, as opposed to just renaming traditional professional services.
zh: 前置部署工程师这个头衔现在超级火，很多做某种企业级业务的公司都声称拥有会去帮客户采用他们所售卖的 SaaS 工具的博士。但你们是这个概念的先驱，对吧？所以我真的很想理解，做前置部署工程到底意味着什么，而不是仅仅把传统专业服务改个名字。

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: I would not call us the pioneers of this. The concept of forward deployed engineering has existed for a very, very long time. Microsoft is the OG of this; they used to do it several decades ago. And the current incarnation of the term was popularized by Palantir back in the 2006, 2007, 2008 time frame, so from 2008 onwards. So we're not the pioneers at all. In fact, we are learning from them and seeing how we take all of that and adapt it to the business we're building. The way I think about it: in any company building and selling a product, there are two things, and everything else is a supporting function. What does selling a product entail? There's the technical selling of it: your typical solution architect or systems engineer persona who comes in, drills through the demos, shows you the use cases, and walks you through the architectures, depending on the product you're selling. So it's technical pieces tied to certain accounts or verticals, and they're incentivized to close the deal. Then there's post-sales, which could be one of two ways: "I'm going to help you implement the thing you bought," or, "Now it's implemented and I'm going to be the service or customer support team, so if something goes wrong, you call us and we'll help you fix it." Note that in both cases, the product team builds something technical, and the go-to-market teams, both pre- and post-sales, go make the customer successful with what the product team built. FDE, forward deployed engineering, is actually different. There are a couple of things that are different from traditional professional services, which is the post-implementation work. One: in typical professional services, I'm going to give you my time and you're going to give me money. The exchange is time and money, and you tell me what you want me to do and I'll do it for you. I'm simplifying it, but generally that's how it works. One of the core parts of FDE is that it's not that I'm going to just give you my time and do whatever you want. It's that we're going to align on an outcome. We might even spend time together to identify the right outcome for the business based on the overall goals. I'm going to align on that, and then I'm in it with you. We're going to make it happen. So there's a lot more ownership in that relationship, as opposed to, "You just tell me what to do and I'm your implementation person." The second component is that whatever work we do will feed back into the product. In Anthropic's case, part of it feeds into the research as well, because that's how you build the flywheel. So FDE as a function is very closely tied to the product and engineering function, and that's where the value gets created. Every engagement should produce a couple of things for us. One, feedback into product. Two, it needs to create some sort of blueprint or playbook, so we don't have to do that type of engagement again. It's a first-of-a-kind, tip-of-the-spear problem that hasn't been solved before. We come in and help solve it, and then that becomes a template that either gets productized, or we give it to customers to build themselves if appropriate, or we give it to partners to scale up. There are a bunch of system integrator partners that will take those templates and say, "This is how you do this in a bank." So that's how we think about it. We're not trying to build or scale a professional services arm. This is essentially to figure out how to bring this technology into the real world in the best possible way, and then take all those learnings, templatize them, and give them away, either as product or as blueprints. The Three Filters for Choosing Customers
zh: 我不会称我们为先驱。前置部署工程的概念已经存在非常非常长的时间了。微软是这个玩法的 OG；他们几十年前就在做了。而这个术语的当前形态是由 Palantir 在 2006、2007、2008 年前后推广开的，也就是从 2008 年起。所以我们完全不是先驱。事实上，我们正在向他们学习，看我们如何把所有这些经验拿来，适配到我们正在打造的业务上。我是这么想的：在任何打造并销售产品的公司里，有两件事，其他一切都是支持性职能。销售一个产品意味着什么？有技术性销售：你典型的解决方案架构师或系统工程师角色，他们进来，反复演示，向你展示使用场景，并根据你在销售的产品带你走一遍架构。所以这是和某些客户或行业绑定的技术性角色，他们的激励是达成交易。然后是售后，它可能是两种方式之一："我要帮你实施你买的东西，" 或者 "现在它已经实施了，我来做服务或客户支持团队，所以如果出了问题，你打电话给我们，我们会帮你修好。" 注意，在这两种情况下，产品团队打造某个技术产品，而面向市场的团队，售前和售后，去用产品团队打造的东西帮客户取得成功。FDE，前置部署工程，实际上是不同的。它有几个地方与传统专业服务不同，后者是实施之后的工作。第一：在典型的专业服务里，我把我的时间给你，你把钱给我。交换的是时间和金钱，你告诉我要做什么，我就为你做。我在简化它，但大体上就是这么运作的。FDE 的核心之一是，并不是我就把我的时间给你、你想让我干什么就干什么。而是我们要在一个成果上达成一致。我们甚至可能会一起花时间，根据整体目标为业务找出正确的成果。我会在那上面达成一致，然后我就和你一起置身其中。我们要把它做成。所以这种关系里有多得多的主人翁意识，而不是 "你只管告诉我要做什么，我就是你的实施人员"。第二个部分是，无论我们做什么工作，都会反馈到产品中。在 Anthropic 的情况下，其中一部分也会反馈到研究中，因为这就是你打造飞轮的方式。所以 FDE 作为一个职能，与产品和工程职能联系非常紧密，而价值正是在那里被创造出来的。每一次合作都应该为我们产出几样东西。第一，对产品的反馈。第二，它需要创造出某种蓝图或打法手册，这样我们就不必再做那种类型的合作了。它是一个首创的、尖刀上的问题，以前从未被解决过。我们进来帮忙解决它，然后它就成为一个模板，要么被产品化，要么在合适的情况下交给客户自己去构建，要么交给合作伙伴去规模化。有很多系统集成商合作伙伴会拿走那些模板然后说："这就是你在一家银行里做这件事的方法。" 我们就是这么想的。我们不是在尝试打造或规模化一个专业服务部门。这本质上是为了弄清楚如何以最好的方式把这项技术带进真实世界，然后把所有这些经验模板化，并把它们送出去，要么作为产品，要么作为蓝图。 选择客户的三个过滤器

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: At the same time, I imagine this service is reserved for a certain level of client, right? Because it's harder to scale such an elite team to go into clients and deploy this type of solution. So what makes the cut?
zh: 同时，我猜这项服务是留给某个层级以上的客户的，对吧？因为要规模化这样一支精英团队、让他们进到客户那里部署这类解决方案，是很难的。那什么样的才能入选？

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: That's a great question. If we look at the definition: one, is the work aligned with our mission as a company, our mission of bringing AI safely to the world, but not just bringing AI to the world, also for the benefit of humanity generally. That's one. Two, is it a first-of-a-kind, and will it open up a set of use cases or a vertical for us that currently isn't available? And three, is there some signal we think we'll get for the product out of this engagement? So we look at those three things and then decide, should we lean in here or not. The FDE team actually does not look at commercials as the only lens. In fact, these three things are much more important than the commercials.
zh: 这是个好问题。如果我们看定义：第一，这项工作是否与作为一家公司的我们的使命一致，也就是把 AI 安全地带给世界的使命，而且不只是把 AI 带给世界，也是为了整个人类的一般福祉。这是一。第二，它是不是首创的，以及它是否会为我们打开一组目前尚不可获得的使用场景或一个行业？第三，这次合作是否能为产品带来某种我们认为会得到的信号？所以我们看这三件事，然后决定，我们要不要在这里投入。FDE 团队实际上并不会把商业回报作为唯一的视角。事实上，这三件事比商业回报重要得多。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: Where do these PhDs come from? Because if you go to LinkedIn, everybody calls themselves either an APM or a forward deployed engineer or whatever they want to call themselves. But realistically, what does it take to become an FDE at Anthropic?
zh: 这些博士是从哪里来的？因为如果你去 LinkedIn，每个人都自称 APM 或者前置部署工程师，或者随他们想叫什么。但现实地说，要成为 Anthropic 的一名 FDE 需要什么？

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: I don't think I can say there's one kind of persona that makes for a good FDE. We've got FDEs who were engineers. We have FDEs who were researchers and have their PhDs. We have FDEs who come from non-engineering backgrounds as well. So the background, while important, is not the only thing that matters. What really matters is mission alignment. Are you hands-on and building things? Can you be in front of customers in complex environments and actually guide them through the journey? Because we have to help them, and oftentimes we don't even know the answers, so we have to go figure it out. Since it's never been done before, we're going to run into problems we never anticipated. So it's: do you have high agency? Are you going to go figure things out and really try to disambiguate, while maintaining the customer relationship, maintaining the trust of the customer, having their back, and doing it in a manner aligned with our culture and mission? That's really what we look for. The Talent Wars and Choosing Mission Over Comp
zh: 我不认为存在某一种固定的画像就能构成一名好的 FDE。我们有曾经是工程师的 FDE。我们有曾经是研究者、拥有博士学位的 FDE。我们也有来自非工程背景的 FDE。所以背景虽然重要，但并不是唯一重要的东西。真正重要的是与使命对齐。你是否亲自动手打造东西？你能否在复杂的环境中面对客户，并真正引导他们走过这段旅程？因为我们必须帮助他们，而且很多时候我们甚至不知道答案，所以我们得去把答案弄清楚。由于这事从来没有被做过，我们会遇到我们从未预料到的问题。所以关键在于：你是否有很高的主观能动性？你是否会去把事情弄清楚，并真正尝试去厘清歧义，同时维护客户关系，维护客户的信任，为他们撑腰，并以符合我们文化和使命的方式来做？这就是我们真正在寻找的东西。 人才战争与选择使命而非报酬

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I want to talk about comp packages too, because I think it's a big elephant in the room. We're hearing how these frontier labs are throwing money at incredible talent, but at the same time, this talent is being poached from one lab to another. As I hear you talk about mission alignment and thinking beyond pure comp, how do you think about retaining this type of talent?
zh: 我也想聊聊薪酬包，因为我觉得这是房间里一头很大的大象。我们听说这些前沿实验室在向了不起的人才砸钱，但与此同时，这些人才正被从一个实验室挖到另一个实验室。听你谈到与使命对齐、超越纯粹报酬的思考，你觉得应该如何留住这类人才？

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: As far as I know, we have not really had a problem from a retention perspective so far. Anthropic has been growing very, very fast, and the stock grants are worth more than what you got three or six months ago. Competition has not been a reason why we've seen any attrition, and Anthropic generally has not seen attrition, from what I understand. Now, again, it's a very young company, so we still have to keep doing what we're doing and keep raising the bar for ourselves. In the long term, this has yet to play out. But we are a very, very principled company, and people who join Anthropic are generally very aligned with that set of principles. That's one of the primary drivers when people join us, and we screen for that in the interview. Having said that, you're right that the comp packages are very generous within the labs, much more so than the FAANG companies, which was not true five or six years ago. The FAANG companies were the biggest, or the healthiest, paymasters. That has definitely changed now.
zh: 据我所知，到目前为止我们在留存方面还真的没有遇到问题。Anthropic 一直在非常非常快地增长，股票授予的价值比你三或六个月前拿到的更高。竞争并不是我们见到任何人员流失的原因，而且据我了解，Anthropic 总体上没有出现人员流失。当然，再说一次，这是一家非常年轻的公司，所以我们仍然必须继续做我们正在做的事，并不断为我们自己提高标准。长期来看，这一切还有待展开。但我们是一家非常、非常有原则的公司，而加入 Anthropic 的人通常都与那套原则高度一致。这是人们加入我们的主要驱动因素之一，而我们在面试中也会筛选这一点。话虽如此，你说得对，实验室内部的薪酬包非常慷慨，比 FAANG 公司还要慷慨得多，而这在五六年前是不成立的。那时候 FAANG 公司是最大的、或者说是最健康的付薪者。现在这一点肯定变了。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I want to share a quick anecdote you and I talked about, and you gave me permission to put it here: in your case, other companies tried to hire you for even more money than Anthropic offered, and you're really one of the few who chose mission over comp, assuming there's a certain level of comp that makes you comfortable enough. So it's true that now a lot of these talented professionals working at the labs are being treated like NBA players, and the comp packages we're seeing are absolutely insane. And I just don't know how long this talent war is going to last.
zh: 我想快速分享一个你我聊过的轶事，你允许我把它放在这里：在你的情况下，其他公司曾试图用比 Anthropic 更多的钱聘请，而你的确是少数几个选择了使命而非报酬的人之一，前提是存在某个让你足够舒适的报酬水平。确实，现在很多在实验室工作的优秀人才正被当成 NBA 球员来对待，我们看到的薪酬包绝对疯狂。而我真不知道这场人才战争还会持续多久。

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: Yes. In my case, there were a couple of opportunities that would have paid more, even two to three times more. My decision criteria was actually very simple. My heart felt pulled in this direction, and historically I have not operated from my heart, I've operated from my mind. This time I wanted to do it differently. My heart pulled in this direction, and I followed it. Why did the heart pull in this direction? Really because I felt connected to the mission, and it resonated. And everybody I met, and how they talked about how the mission and principles actually play out in practice on a day-to-day basis, that resonated for me. So that's why I chose this direction. In terms of the talent wars, my line of thinking is: if AI is to play out all the benefits we talk about, ranging from medicine to bio research to chemicals to everything, then the understanding of AI, especially on the applied side, has to be taken to the market, and there needs to be diffusion of it. Otherwise, if it only remains with a small set of people, AI will not play out at the scale of humanity. It will remain concentrated among a very small group, and limited to the impact that small group can have. So I believe it's our job and our responsibility to diffuse this: to train people, to teach, to make it easier to deploy, to make it easier to build, and so on. And that's very much part of Anthropic's line of thinking. If you start to think about open weights models, that's another form of diffusion. These capabilities are not all just behind paywalls now; you have to pay for infrastructure, but you have these open weights models, and you have choice available to you. So that's another form of diffusion happening. The same thing has to happen with talent. If you look historically, in the late 90s website developers were rare, and they used to charge a bomb. Well, today you just go to any of these tools, you go to Lovable and type one single thing, and it's going to give you a full app. So diffusion happens in every industry over time, and it's going to happen here as well. Winning the Game vs. Seeing Its Futility
zh: 是的。在我的情况下，有几个机会本可以付得更多，甚至是两到三倍。我的决策标准其实非常简单。我的内心被拉向了这个方向，而从历史上看，我一直不是凭内心行事的，我是凭头脑行事的。这一次我想用不同的方式来做。我的内心把我拉向了这个方向，而我跟随了它。为什么内心被拉向这个方向？真的是因为我感到与使命相连，它让我产生了共鸣。还有我遇见的每一个人，以及他们如何谈论使命和原则在日常实践中是如何真正落地的，这对我产生了共鸣。所以这就是我选择这个方向的原因。至于人才战争，我的思路是：如果 AI 要兑现我们所谈到的所有好处，从医学到生物研究到化学到一切，那么对 AI 的理解，尤其是在应用侧的理解，必须被带到市场上，并且需要有它的扩散。否则，如果它只留在一小撮人手里，AI 就不会在人类的尺度上兑现。它将保持集中在非常小的一群人中，并且仅限于那一小群人所能产生的影响。所以我相信，扩散它是我们的工作和责任：去培训人们、去教学、让部署更容易、让构建更容易，等等。而这正是 Anthropic 思路中非常重要的一部分。如果你开始想想开放权重模型，那是另一种形式的扩散。这些能力现在并非全都躲在付费墙后面；你得为基础设施付费，但你有这些开放权重模型，你有选择权。所以那是正在发生的另一种形式的扩散。同样的事情也必须发生在人才上。如果你回顾历史，90 年代末网站开发者很稀缺，他们收费高得吓人。而今天，你只要打开这些工具中的任何一个，你打开 Lovable，输入一句话，它就会给你一个完整的应用。所以扩散会随着时间在每一个行业发生，而它也终将在这里发生。 赢得游戏 versus 看清它的徒劳

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: I want to acknowledge, as I hear you talk about the decisions you've been able to make, that you earned the right and the privilege to make them: to not take an offer that's double what you're making, or to decide to be an IC and then a manager. I see a lot of people who are fighting their way up, let's call it director level, and they say, "Yeah, right, but in reality I really want that 2x package, and I really want to be a CPO." So I'm curious how you think about it from the perspective of someone who has achieved certain things in life and is now in a position to be more free to choose their next move.
zh: 听你谈到你所做出的那些决定，我想先确认一点：你赢得了做出这些决定的权利和特权：不接一份薪水是你两倍的 offer，或者决定先做 IC 再做管理者。我看到很多人正在向上拼杀，姑且叫总监级别，他们说："是啊，对，但实际上我真的想要那份两倍的薪酬包，我真的想成为 CPO。" 所以我很好奇，从一个已经在人生中取得了一些成就、现在处于更自由地选择下一步的位置的人的角度，你是怎么想的。

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: Naval Ravikant says this: that to be free of a game, you have to first win the game, and only then do you realize the futility of the game, and then you're free of it. I think he's right, but only partly right. It's 90% right. The thing that's missing is that to realize the futility of the game, there are a number of other ways you can get there; it's not just winning the game. You can realize the futility of the game in other ways. How I realized the futility of the game was as I reflected on my journey. I wasn't a director at Amazon, I wasn't a VP at Amazon, for instance. So it's not that I got to VP and then said, "What's the big deal, I can just give this up." I was very much on that ladder of growth, for that definition of growth. But I also found myself just not any happier as I grew. It just kind of wasn't cutting it. Then I had a few experiences that made me go through this thinking: I went from point A to point B, I didn't feel any different. I went from point A to point C, I didn't feel any different. What were the things missing for me at each of these points? I started to see a consistency for myself: there was just not enough heart involved in each of those steps. So that realization, over several years, not overnight, led me to this place of, "I've got to at least give it a shot and see what happens. I owe it to myself to let my heart be the leader here." Now, it doesn't hurt that the company is Anthropic. It doesn't hurt that they pay well. So I'm not compromising on anything from a quality-of-life perspective. If anything, it's an awesome brand and a fantastic group of people. So I won't say I'm free of the game; that's not the right characterization. I can see the futility of it, but I haven't freed myself of it.
zh: Naval Ravikant 说过这句话：要摆脱一个游戏，你必须先赢得这个游戏，只有到那时你才会意识到这个游戏的徒劳，然后你才能从中解脱。我认为他是对的，但只对了一部分。90% 是对的。缺失的地方在于，要意识到游戏的徒劳，还有许多其他途径可以到达那里；不仅仅是赢得游戏。你可以通过其他方式意识到游戏的徒劳。我自己意识到游戏徒劳的方式，是当我回顾我的旅程时。比如，我不是亚马逊的总监，也不是亚马逊的 VP。所以我并不是做到了 VP 然后说："这有什么大不了的，我随时可以放弃这些。" 我当年完全在那条成长的梯子上，按照那个对成长的定义。但我也发现自己随着晋升并没有变得更快乐。它就是不太够。然后我经历了几次让我进行这种思考的体验：我从 A 点到 B 点，我没有感到任何不同。我从 A 点到 C 点，我没有感到任何不同。在每一个这样的节点上，我缺的是什么？我开始为自己看到一个一致性：在每一个这样的台阶上，参与的内心都太少了。所以那个领悟，历经数年，而不是一夜之间，把我带到了这个地方："我至少得试一试，看看会发生什么。我欠我自己一个机会，让我的内心在这里做领导者。" 当然，这家公司是 Anthropic 也无妨。他们付高薪也无妨。所以从生活质量的 perspective 我并没有在任何事情上妥协。如果非要说，它是一个很棒的品牌和一群很出色的人。所以我不会说我已经摆脱了游戏；那不是准确的描述。我能看到它的徒劳，但我还没有把自己从中解放出来。

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: The way I think about it is that ultimately you have the freedom to create your own game. Sure, there are certain parameters in life that are predefined; if you want to live in certain parts of the world, you need to make a certain amount of money. But at the same time, someone defined what a level two, three, four, or five is at a company. And maybe at some point you say, "What if I define those levels for my own company, or for my own life?"
zh: 我的想法是，归根结底你有创造自己游戏的自由。当然，生活中有一些参数是预先定好的；如果你想住在世界上某些地方，你就需要赚到一定数目的钱。但与此同时，某个人定义了公司里的二级、三级、四级或五级是什么。也许在某个时候你会说："如果我为自己的公司，或者为我自己的生活来定义那些级别呢？"

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: Totally, absolutely. What you're pointing to is incredibly important. I certainly got wrapped up in the game that was defined by somebody else. The rules were defined by somebody else, what good looks like is defined by somebody else, and some of those things just did not align with how I saw the world and the life I wanted to live. For instance, I value health and community. If I need to be a VP at any company and work 60 hours a week, I won't be able to pay attention to my community, my family, and my health. That's just how it is. And you see this, right? I don't want to be 70 years old, sick, not very healthy, sitting on $50 million. That trade just didn't make sense to me. So that's an example of me observing the game, evaluating it for myself, and saying, "Does this fit me?" And it just didn't fit me. Why Everyone at Anthropic Shares One Title
zh: 完全如此，绝对是这样。你所指向的东西极其重要。我确实曾被别人定义的游戏缠住过。规则是别人定义的，什么是好是别人定义的，而其中一些东西就是和我看待世界的方式、以及我想要过的生活不一致。比如，我重视健康和社群。如果我需要在任何一家公司当 VP 并且每周工作 60 个小时，我就无法顾及我的社群、我的家人和我的健康。事实就是这样。而你也见过这种情况，对吧？我不想在 70 岁的时候，生病，身体不太健康，守着 5000 万美元坐着。这笔交易对我来说就是不合理。所以那就是我观察这个游戏、为我自己评估它、然后问 "这适合我吗？" 的一个例子。而它就是不适合我。 为什么 Anthropic 人人共享一个头衔

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
en: One of the mechanisms I think Anthropic is using, which is very smart, is that everybody is a Member of Technical Staff. So tell me more about it. How are people okay with using the same term regardless of level?
zh: 我认为 Anthropic 正在使用的机制之一，非常聪明，就是人人都是技术组成员。那么跟我多讲讲这个。人们怎么能接受无论级别高低都使用同一个术语？

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: This is a culture thing, and people self-select into it. If I'm in a meeting with somebody who would have been a VP, let's say I'm at Amazon in a meeting with a VP, I'm in a meeting with the VP. Their word carries more weight than my word. There's an implicit authority relationship there. At Anthropic, I'm in a meeting with Andrej Karpathy, an absolute celebrity, so deep in the space, someone so many people look up to, including me. When he introduces himself, sure, I know who Andrej is, but he's an MTS and I'm an MTS. So the titles almost don't matter. Now, let's assume I didn't know who Andrej is, that I was living under a rock and had never heard his name. I'm in a meeting with him, having a discussion. Titles? His says MTS, mine says MTS. I look him up in the company directory: MTS. So we're on equal footing in that conversation. It's all about that conversation, what you're bringing to it, adding value to it, and having respect for the other individual, not because of their title, but because of their ideas. So people just bring it; people self-select into it. That's why I don't have a problem with the title. I'm an MTS, the people who report to me are MTS, I report to an MTS. Yeah, okay, whatever.
zh: 这是一个文化上的事情，而且人们会自我选择加入它。如果我和某个本该是 VP 的人开会，比方说我在亚马逊和一位 VP 开会，我是在和 VP 开会。他的话比我的话更有分量。那里存在一种隐性的权威关系。在 Anthropic，我和 Andrej Karpathy 开会，他是一位绝对的明星人物，在这个领域浸淫极深，是许许多多人仰望的对象，包括我。当他自我介绍时，当然，我知道 Andrej 是谁，但他是一名 MTS，我也是一名 MTS。所以头衔几乎不重要。好，现在假设我不知道 Andrej 是谁，假设我一直住在石头底下，从来没听说过他的名字。我和他开会讨论。头衔？他的写着 MTS，我的写着 MTS。我在公司通讯录里查他：MTS。所以在那场对话中我们是平等的地位。一切都关于那场对话本身，你为它带来了什么，为它增添价值，并且尊重对方这个人，不是因为他头衔，而是因为他的想法。所以人们自然而然就这样做；人们自我选择加入它。这就是为什么我对这个头衔没有意见。我是一名 MTS，向我汇报的人是 MTS，我向一名 MTS 汇报。行吧，都行。

speaker: Amandeep Khurana
en: Thank you. This was a blast, and thank you for the opportunity.
